dataset_family: Cheikh (Sheikh) Khalifa Ibn Zaid Hospital prospective T2DM cohort, Casablanca, Morocco: 100 patients recruited May-September 2021. It is the same cohort as Rhmari Tlemcani et al. 2022 (Cureus), which is not in the corpus. No other corpus block reports it.
method_family: Classical AutoML (PyCaret; best model Extra Trees) on 21 routine clinical and laboratory variables. Diabetic retinopathy enters as one binary yes/no comorbidity. Random 95%/5% then 70/30 split, recursive feature elimination and SHAP ranking. MCI defined by MMSE alone. No ocular measurement is acquired or analysed.
what_it_shows:
Rhmari Tlemcani et al. 2025, PLOS One.
- In 100 people with T2DM (MCI prevalence 47.5% by MMSE), an Extra Trees classifier on routine variables reached test-set accuracy 0.8276 (AUC 0.8619 with all features, 0.8952 after RFE). The headline figures are accuracy 0.9310 and AUC 0.9667 on the 'unseen data'.
- In the SHAP plot, diabetic retinopathy (present in 39%) was the top-ranked contributor, followed by age, microalbuminuria, LDL, HbA1c and creatinine.
- The paper also reports that no variable had a significant linear correlation with MCI.
- No retinal imaging, retinal measurement or eye-movement recording is analysed, and the extract does not state how DR was ascertained.
why:
PDF identity confirmed. The title, the authors (Rhmari Tlemcani, Aitlahbib, Laidi, Alidrissi, Aasfara, Elamari, Chadli, Motaib) and DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0332442 match the block. I read the whole extract (pp.1-11, up to the References).

STATED FORM, no. The study does not test an ocular channel. Diabetic retinopathy is a binary clinical-complication field in a 21-variable table of routine data. No retinal structure is imaged or measured, and the extract never says how DR status was determined (no fundus, ophthalmologic or grading method is described; a grep for these terms finds nothing). 'DR is the top SHAP feature' is a feature-importance ranking inside one multivariable model fitted on 100 people. It is not an estimated association with a confidence interval. The paper's own exploratory analysis found that 'No variable showed a significant linear correlation with the target parameter MCI' (p.3), and that includes DR. MCI is defined by MMSE alone (p.2). So the study neither shows retinal structure as a biomarker channel nor bears on scalability.

The performance figures are also internally inconsistent. This is my arithmetic, not the paper's. The 'unseen data' is described as 5% of 100 patients, about 5 people (p.3). An accuracy of 0.9310 is impossible on 5 cases, where only multiples of 0.2 can occur. It equals 27/29. The test-set values 0.8276 (24/29) and 0.7931 (23/29) also imply a 29-patient denominator. The block's 'Accuracy 0.9310, AUC 0.9667' is therefore the paper's headline, but the paper cannot have obtained it on the set it describes. The authors themselves flag a small single-hospital sample and a risk of overfitting (p.10).

NARROWED FORM, no. The narrowed wording concerns ocular measures (retinal imaging, saccadic measures). This study analyses no ocular measure.

INDEPENDENCE. Moroccan single-hospital T2DM cohort. No shared sample, site or authors with P-5, P-952, P-966 or P-105. None with the candidates P-255 (EU RECOGNISED T2D, a different population and continent), P-224 (Qatar) or P-830 (a synthesis closed 2021, before this 2025 study). Not a preprint: a peer-reviewed article in PLOS One.

quotes.quote: The dataset included 100 patients. Extra Trees classifier was the best-performing model for mild cognitive impairment (Accuracy: 0·9310/AUC: 0·9667/ Recall: 0·9333/ Precision: 0·9333/F1: 0·9333). The most contributing factors to MCI in patients with type 2 diabetes were, respectively, diabetic retinopathy, age, serum LDL cholesterol level, microalbuminuria, HbA1c, and, serum creatinine level.
The primary outcome being predicted in this study is MCI, assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), a widely used cognitive screening tool.
The dataset comprises 21 variables and 100 records. The target parameter “MCI” is balanced (47%/53%). ... No variable showed a significant linear correlation with the target parameter “MCI”.

The data was randomly divided into two parts. The first part, which represented 95% of the data, was then split into two sections: 70% was used as the training set and 30% as the test set. Machine learning models were trained using the training dataset, and their performance was assessed on the test dataset. The remaining 5% of the total data, referred to as the ‘unseen data’, was reserved for final validation.
These models are the Extra Trees Classifier (Accuracy: 0·8276/AUC: 0·8952/Recall: 0·8667/Precision: 0·8125/F1: 0·8387)

As a final step, we used the unseen dataset with the validated trained model to predict MCI, using the best performing model, Extra Trees Classifier. This model achieved an accuracy of 0·9310, an AUC of 0·9667, a recall of 0·9333, a precision of 0·9333, and, an F1 score of 0·9333.
Diabetic retinopathy was the predominant factor, with an increased risk of MCI in patients diagnosed with this condition compared to those without it.
Table 1. Descriptive characteristics of the study population (n = 100). ... Diabetic retinopathy, n (%) 39 (39%)

The limitations of our study include the relatively small sample size from a single hospital and the extensive use of variables. While this approach is beneficial for predictive accuracy, it could also lead to overfitting, despite our precautions.
